query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled thermomechanical processing step to produce serrated, non‐planar colony boundaries in the dual-phase lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy will both suppress microcrack nucleation at the internal interfaces and enhance work hardening, leading to simultaneous improvements in yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventional, as‐cast microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (for example, AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure that features relatively straight, continuous colony (and phase) boundaries where microcracking initiates during tensile deformation at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical treatment—such as moderate cold rolling (e.g., an 8–10% thickness reduction) immediately followed by an annealing step at an optimized temperature—to induce a serrated, wavy interfacial morphology in the lamellar colonies.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under ambient conditions with standard strain rates (e.g., approximately 10⁻³ s⁻¹) to compare the mechanical response of treated versus conventionally processed samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of serrated colony and phase boundaries that, by introducing local geometric irregularities, promote crack deflection and blunting, and result in a more heterogeneous stress distribution across the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The serrated interfaces act as effective crack arresters by increasing the energy required for a crack to propagate along a tortuous path. In addition, the heterogeneous microstructure improves load transfer and enhances strain hardening. Together these effects suppress the premature formation and coalescence of microcracks, thereby raising the yield strength while also extending tensile ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, straight-boundary baseline, the serrated-boundary alloy is expected to show a moderate, statistically significant increase in both yield strength and tensile elongation. While exact numerical improvements are uncertain, the intervention should demonstrably delay crack initiation and slow crack propagation, leading to improved overall damage tolerance.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with straight, continuous lamellar and colony boundaries that promote rapid microcrack initiation and brittle-type failure during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: This strategy is expected to be effective provided that (a) the alloy’s dual-phase lamellar structure is preserved and (b) the processing parameters (rolling reduction and annealing temperature/time) are carefully tuned so as not to induce unwanted coarsening or loss of phase stability. Its effectiveness is specifically applicable to eutectic HEAs with microstructures dominated by lamellar colonies rather than to alloys with entirely different morphologies.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement is not precisely predictable without experimental calibration. The sensitivity of serration formation to processing conditions and the potential influence on phase stability represent areas of uncertainty that require systematic parameter optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the same eutectic HEA alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1). The control batch is produced by conventional casting without further thermomechanical modification. The experimental batch is subjected to a controlled process consisting of moderate cold rolling (approximately 8–10% reduction) immediately followed by annealing at an optimized temperature (to be determined by preliminary trials) that promotes the development of serrated colony boundaries. Microstructural characterization (SEM, EBSD) is performed to confirm the presence and degree of boundary serration. Then, both batches are tested under identical room-temperature tensile conditions (standard strain rate, ambient atmosphere).
measurements: SEM/EBSD imaging to quantify the degree and morphology of boundary serration
Room-temperature tensile tests to record yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure
Fractographic analysis to assess crack initiation and propagation paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., at least a 10% increase) improvement in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the control, or if the fracture surfaces and crack propagation patterns remain essentially unchanged (i.e., showing similar microcrack initiation and propagation along straight interfaces), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
